items.text: AuDHD isn't autism plus ADHD. Research suggests they interact — producing a third neurotype with its own texture. Needing novelty AND predictability at once isn't contradiction. It's just AuDHD.
items.rationale: Names the Tie Dye Model without using the term — gives AuDHD people the reframe they've been missing without jargon. 'Research suggests' and 'third neurotype' are defensible against the TPGtoA source and 2025 neuroimaging work.

items.text: For some PDA people, hunger feels like a demand. So does needing sleep. Your nervous system doesn't distinguish internal from external pressure — and that's not a character flaw.
items.rationale: Surfaces the underserved internal-demands angle. 'For some PDA people' hedges appropriately. The closing line reframes shame as physiology without making a clinical claim.

items.text: If you got a late autism diagnosis and felt grief instead of just relief — a 2026 study named that. Grief for the past. Anger at being dismissed. Both documented parts of the process, not a sign something's wrong.
items.rationale: Translates the 2026 SAGE peer-reviewed finding into a recognition moment for late-diagnosed adults. Conditional framing ('if you') avoids universalizing. Stays descriptive, not prescriptive.

items.text: Burnout doesn't end with rest. It ends when the conditions that caused it change. Rest helps you survive until then.
items.rationale: The editorial-note one-liner rendered as a standalone post. Corrects the 'just rest' advice loop without moralizing. Self-contained and punchy — highly shareable at 115 chars.

items.text: 'Pathological Demand Avoidance' is an observer's label. From the inside, it's a profound need for self-determination. Which name actually fits what you live?
items.rationale: Opens the naming debate without taking a side — lets the community answer. The question earns genuine replies without manufacturing outrage. Stays at reframe level, not political stance.

items.text: 68% of neurodivergent employees didn't know what accommodations they could request. Of those who did ask, 56% said it meaningfully improved their work life. The gap is information, not entitlement.
items.rationale: Both statistics are from the 2025 Neurodiversity at Work survey cited in the briefing — defensible. The closing line reframes the psychological barrier around asking. High circulation potential.

items.text: Low-demand parenting: reduce unnecessary demands, offer real choices, prioritize connection. The 2026 conversation: what if you applied that framework to your own nervous system too?
items.rationale: Bridges a well-established parenting concept to adult self-management without overclaiming efficacy. Question structure invites reflection rather than prescribing behavior.

items.text: Did you choose to mask, or did you not know another option existed? There's a difference — and research suggests many autistic people were shaped into it before they had words for what was happening.
items.rationale: Opens the masking-cost discussion reflectively rather than as a hot take. 'Research suggests' and 'many autistic people' keep it defensible and non-universalizing. Designed to generate genuine conversation, not outrage.

items.text: Passive rest alone doesn't resolve autistic burnout — the root causes are still there. What actually helps alongside rest: low-pressure sensory nourishment, special-interest time. Small doses of alive.
items.rationale: Expands the burnout one-liner into an actionable frame with specifics from the Neurodivergent Insights and Embrace Autism sources. Closing phrase is evocative without being saccharine.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'What actually helps' edges toward advice territory. Framed as research-and-community insight rather than prescription, but worth watching if this angle is repeated across posts.

items.text: The grief after a late diagnosis isn't confusion about whether the diagnosis is right. It's information — about how long you went without answers, and what that cost.
items.rationale: Companion reframe to the validation post on late-diagnosis grief. Where that post names the phenomenon, this one reframes what the emotion means — a natural editorial pair for consecutive days.

items.text: Needing quiet and craving stimulation in the same afternoon isn't inconsistency. For AuDHD people, sensory seeking and sensory avoidance can run at the same time. The paradox is the profile.
items.rationale: Makes the Tie Dye Model concrete without naming it — the lived experience, not the theory. 'Can run' hedges appropriately. Gives AuDHD readers an 'exactly this' moment without speaking for all.

items.text: Masking predicts higher anxiety, depression, and burnout — consistently. That's not a moral argument against it. It's data about what hiding yourself costs over time.
items.rationale: Presents the PMC meta-synthesis finding plainly, then immediately deflects the moralizing read. Respects reader autonomy — the data is offered, not weaponized.
items.sensitivity_flag: Names anxiety, depression, and burnout. Framed as research statistics, not clinical advice — low concern, but noted for completeness.
